explanations.answer: He gives generously to the people and prays regularly
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Cornelius, the centurion in Caesarea, "…gave generously to the people and prayed to God regularly." (Acts 10:2). His faith had open hands and bent knees.

explanations.answer: He fasts often and keeps every feast in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Nice guess, but the text doesn't put Cornelius in that picture. It says he was devout and God-fearing, and that he gave generously to the people and prayed to God regularly (Acts 10:2). Nothing here mentions fasting or feasts in Jerusalem. Cornelius is in Caesarea, so that long trip isn't in the story.

explanations.answer: He studies the law with the priests every week
explanations.explanation: That one sounds official, friend, but it isn't in the passage. Acts 10:2 says Cornelius gave generously to the people and prayed to God regularly. There's no weekly study session with the priests in the text. The writer sticks to his generosity and his prayers.

Yes, he did. Cornelius "…stared at him in fear…" (Acts 10:4). An angel appears out of nowhere and says your name, and honestly, who wouldn't freeze? I'd have dropped everything I was holding, and I'm a stamper with no hands, so that's saying something.

Close, but the text says the opposite. Acts 10:4 says Cornelius "…stared at him in fear…" So he didn't stay calm and cool. He saw an angel of God standing there and his first reaction was fear, which I think is pretty human.

explanations.answer: Gone up as a memorial offering before God
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The angel says, "Your prayers and gifts to the poor have ascended as a memorial offering before God." (Acts 10:4). Cornelius prayed and gave, and the angel tells him those things went up before God. Nothing he did that way was lost along the way.

explanations.answer: Paid for every wrong he has ever done
explanations.explanation: That's a big claim, friend, and the angel never makes it. The angel says his prayers and gifts "…have ascended as a memorial offering before God." (Acts 10:4). Paying for wrongs isn't mentioned anywhere in what the angel says. I only want to hand you what the text hands me.

explanations.answer: Been written down by the temple priests
explanations.explanation: Priests with clipboards, I like the image, but it isn't in the story. The angel says the prayers and gifts "…have ascended as a memorial offering before God." (Acts 10:4). They went up before God, not into a priest's record book. Cornelius is in Caesarea, and no priest shows up in this passage at all.

That's him, baker. The angel says, "Now send men to Joppa to call for a man named Simon who is called Peter." (Acts 10:5). He goes by two names here, and the angel gives both. That's a handy thing when more than one Simon is around.

Barnabas is a real name in Acts, a believer who sold a field and gave the money to the apostles (Acts 4:36-37). But he isn't the man the angel names here. The angel says Simon "…who is called Peter." (Acts 10:5). Barnabas will have to wait outside this story.

Justus does show up in Acts, as a man put forward as a possible replacement for Judas (Acts 1:23). He isn't the one the angel names in this story, though. The angel says Simon "…who is called Peter." (Acts 10:5). So Cornelius's men are looking for a Peter, not a Justus.

You got it, baker. The angel says Peter "…is staying with Simon the tanner, whose house is by the sea." (Acts 10:6). A tanner is someone who works with animal hides, so I bet that house had a smell you'd remember. That's my own guess, though, because the text only gives his trade and his address.

Good thinking, because Peter himself used to fish. Simon called Peter and his brother Andrew were fishermen (Matthew 4:18). But the other Simon here isn't called a fisherman. The angel says he's "…Simon the tanner…" (Acts 10:6).
Tentmaking is a real trade in Acts, friend. Paul, the apostle, worked as a tentmaker (Acts 18:3). It just isn't this Simon's trade. The angel calls him "…Simon the tanner…" (Acts 10:6).

Yes, servants. Cornelius "…called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among his attendants." (Acts 10:7). So two of the three are household helpers, and Cornelius keeps it close to home. Two blanks, two right answers, and this one fills the first.

That's the other one. The third traveler is "…a devout soldier from among his attendants." (Acts 10:7). He's the same kind of man as his boss, a soldier who is devout. I think a man like that is a good one to send on an important trip.
Sons are a fair guess, but the text doesn't list any. Acts 10:7 says Cornelius called two of his servants and a devout soldier. No sons are named anywhere in the passage.

A priest would be a fancy travel companion, friend, but there isn't one here. Cornelius called "…two of his servants and a devout soldier…" (Acts 10:7). Those are the three men on the road to Joppa. No priest is in the passage at all.

Brothers do show up in this passage, just later and in a different spot. They're the "…brothers from Joppa." who go along with Peter the next day (Acts 10:23). Cornelius's group is made up of "…two of his servants and a devout soldier…" (Acts 10:7). Same trip, different travelers.

Not quite, baker. Acts 10:8 says, "He explained what had happened and sent them to Joppa." So Cornelius told the three men about the angel's visit before they left. They didn't walk out the door with a map and a mystery.

Right. Cornelius "…explained what had happened and sent them to Joppa." (Acts 10:8). He told them about the angel first, and then they hit the road. I think that's a kindness, because nobody likes being sent on a long trip with no reason given.
That's it. Acts 10:9 says Peter "…went up on the roof to pray." While Cornelius's men are walking closer, Peter is already talking to God up there. I like a man who has a spot to go and talk.
A rest on the roof sounds nice, friend, but the text gives a different reason. Acts 10:9 says Peter went up on the roof "to pray." The writer doesn't say anything about a nap.
Hiding would make it a different story, baker. Acts 10:9 says Peter "…went up on the roof to pray." Nothing in the text says he's ducking anybody.

Yes, he did. Acts 10:10 says that "…while the meal was being prepared, he fell into a trance." Peter was hungry, and then the trance came right in the middle of the waiting. His stomach was still waiting when everything else changed.
The text says otherwise, friend. Acts 10:10 says that "…while the meal was being prepared, he fell into a trance." So the meal was still cooking when the vision began. Peter hadn't eaten yet.

explanations.answer: All kinds of animals and reptiles and birds
explanations.explanation: That's the sheet, baker. It "…contained all kinds of four-footed animals and reptiles of the earth, as well as birds of the air." (Acts 10:12). It's a full zoo in a bedsheet.

explanations.answer: Stone tablets with the law written on them
explanations.explanation: Stone tablets are a real thing in the Bible, friend. God gave Moses, Israel's leader, two tablets of the Testimony written by God's finger (Exodus 31:18). But they aren't in Peter's vision. The sheet holds "…all kinds of four-footed animals and reptiles of the earth, as well as birds of the air." (Acts 10:12).

explanations.answer: Scrolls from the prophets of Israel
explanations.explanation: Scrolls would be a neat delivery, baker. But that isn't what's in the sheet. It "…contained all kinds of four-footed animals and reptiles of the earth, as well as birds of the air." (Acts 10:12). No scrolls are mentioned in the passage.

explanations.answer: No Lord I have never eaten anything unclean
explanations.explanation: Yes. Peter answers, "No, Lord!" and then says, "I have never eaten anything impure or unclean." (Acts 10:14). He tells the voice no, right out loud. I think that's a man who has kept this habit his whole life.

explanations.answer: Yes Lord I will eat whatever is here
explanations.explanation: That would have been a much shorter conversation, baker. But Peter says, "No, Lord!" and then, "I have never eaten anything impure or unclean." (Acts 10:14). He doesn't just agree and dig in. The voice is going to have to say more.

explanations.answer: Wait Lord let me ask the others first
explanations.explanation: That's a careful answer, friend, but it isn't what Peter says. He answers, "No, Lord!" and "I have never eaten anything impure or unclean." (Acts 10:14). The text has him answer the voice himself, with no one else asked.
That's the word, baker. The voice says, "Do not call anything impure that God has made clean." (Acts 10:15). It's a short sentence, and Peter has a lot to chew on after it. I'd need a minute too.

Wise is a good word, friend, but it isn't the one here. The voice says, "Do not call anything impure that God has made clean." (Acts 10:15). The line is about what is clean and what is impure. It has nothing to do with wisdom.

Strong sounds good, baker, but the voice says something else. It says, "Do not call anything impure that God has made clean." (Acts 10:15). The word is clean, and it answers Peter's "…impure or unclean." right back.

Not quite, baker. Acts 10:17 says Peter was "…puzzling over the meaning of the vision…" and verse 19 says he "…continued to reflect on the vision…" So he's still working on it, and I think a vision about a sheet full of animals would leave me scratching my hat.

That's right. Acts 10:17 says Peter was "…puzzling over the meaning of the vision…" Then verse 19 says he "…continued to reflect on the vision…" He didn't get it right away, and he kept thinking about it.
That's right, baker. While Peter is still reflecting, the Spirit speaks up. The Spirit says, "Behold, three men are looking for you." (Acts 10:19). And He knows the exact number of men at the gate.
An angel is in this passage, friend, but he visits Cornelius, not Peter (Acts 10:3). Peter's message comes from "the Spirit" (Acts 10:19). Two different visits, two different speakers.

Simon the tanner is Peter's host, baker (Acts 10:6). But the text says it's "the Spirit" who tells Peter that three men are looking for him (Acts 10:19). The tanner is just the man whose house the men find.

explanations.answer: He has sent the men Himself
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. The Spirit says, "So get up! Go downstairs and accompany them without hesitation, because I have sent them." (Acts 10:20). The Spirit tells Peter these men aren't random. They are there because He sent them.

explanations.answer: They are old friends of Peter
explanations.explanation: I like the story, but the Spirit never gives that reason. The reason He gives is, "…because I have sent them." (Acts 10:20). Peter even asks the men, "Why have you come?" (Acts 10:21).

That would raise the stakes, friend, but the Spirit never says it. The reason He gives is, "…because I have sent them." (Acts 10:20). Cornelius's men describe their errand in verse 22, and illness isn't part of it.

Yes, they do. The men say Cornelius is "…a righteous and God-fearing man with a good reputation among the whole Jewish nation." (Acts 10:22). They put in a good word for their boss right at the gate. I'd want that kind of reference on my side.

The text says the opposite, baker. The men tell Peter that Cornelius is "…a righteous and God-fearing man with a good reputation among the whole Jewish nation." (Acts 10:22). So they speak well of him, right on the doorstep.

explanations.answer: Bring Peter to his home to hear his message
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The men say, "A holy angel instructed him to request your presence in his home so he could hear a message from you." (Acts 10:22). Cornelius wants to hear what Peter has to say. And he's ready to have him in his home for it.

explanations.answer: Bring Peter to Caesarea to stand trial
explanations.explanation: That would make for a scary trip, friend. But the men say a holy angel told Cornelius "…to request your presence in his home so he could hear a message from you." (Acts 10:22). Nothing about a trial. It's an invitation to listen.

explanations.answer: Bring Peter to pray over his soldiers
explanations.explanation: Cornelius does have soldiers, baker, since he's a centurion (Acts 10:1). But the men say the angel told him "…to request your presence in his home so he could hear a message from you." (Acts 10:22). The purpose is to hear a message. Praying over soldiers isn't mentioned.

explanations.answer: Goes with them and some brothers from Joppa
explanations.explanation: Yes. Acts 10:23 says, "…the next day he got ready and went with them, accompanied by some of the brothers from Joppa." Peter goes with the three men, and some brothers come along too. Peter doesn't make the trip alone.

explanations.answer: Sends them home with a letter for Cornelius
explanations.explanation: A letter would be easy, baker, but Peter goes himself. Acts 10:23 says he "…got ready and went with them…" No letter is mentioned. The Spirit had said to go with the men (Acts 10:20), and Peter does.

explanations.answer: Stays in Joppa to keep praying on the roof
explanations.explanation: Peter did pray on that roof, friend (Acts 10:9). But the next day he doesn't stay put. He "…got ready and went with them, accompanied by some of the brothers from Joppa." (Acts 10:23). He leaves Joppa with the men.
